report.answer_text:
Syria isn't in one single war right now. The large civil war ended, but several smaller conflicts are still going.
Background
The conflict began in 2011 as a civil uprising against President Bashar al-Assad, inspired by the Arab Spring protests.[1] It grew into a full civil war involving many factions and foreign powers.
Rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham took Damascus on 8 December 2024, ending Assad's rule. The group's leader, Ahmed al-Sharaa, was named interim president in January 2025.[2]
The UN-mandated Commission of Inquiry says more than 580,000 people were killed and 13 million were forcibly displaced.[3]
Who is fighting now, and why
1. The government and the Kurdish-led SDF (northeast). The government wants to bring the SDF under the national army's command. Clashes erupted in Aleppo in January 2026 after talks stalled over a missed deadline for integrating the SDF into the army.[3] A US-mediated ceasefire followed on January 30, 2026, though integration is still being negotiated.[4] One tracker reports that SDF commander Mazloum Abdi declared his force dissolved into the national army on 25 August 2026.[2]
2. Israel (south). Israeli forces have run a de facto buffer zone near the Golan Heights since December 8, 2024, moving beyond the 1974 disengagement line.[4] Israeli incursions into southern Syria have escalated since Assad fell.[3] Israeli raids continue in Quneitra and Deraa.[2]
3. Communal and armed groups in the south. There is intermittent fighting between Druze, Bedouin and other armed groups.[3] Sweida has seen renewed violence.
4. Islamic State remnants. Jordanian air strikes hit southern Syria on October 26, 2026. Syria says seven people were killed. Jordan says it killed more than 20 Islamic State militants.[2] Other sources describe a residual fight against IS, and Turkish security concerns also affect the northeast.
5. Leftover Assad-era forces. Transitional authorities have been working to dissolve remnants of Assad's government.[3]
Summary: Syria's government is not at war with another country in the conventional sense. Its main conflicts are with Kurdish-led forces over control and integration, and with Israeli military incursions in the south. It also faces internal sectarian violence and an ongoing counter-ISIS fight. Syria is better described as unstable than fully at peace.[5]
I can go into more detail on any of these if you'd like.
